headline_marked: [[Android Auto may get Work Mode]] for employer-managed apps, discovered in teardown
headline: Android Auto may get Work Mode for employer-managed apps, discovered in teardown
summary: A hidden Work Mode tile was found in an Android Auto teardown, hinting at future support for employer-managed apps and potentially blurring work-life boundaries on your commute.
details: An Android Authority teardown of Android Auto version 18.0.664204 revealed a hidden Work Mode tile. This suggests Google is testing new Work Profile controls, which could bring employer-managed apps to your car's display. The tile, when brought up, showed a briefcase icon but was not functional.

Work Profiles separate employer-managed apps and data from personal apps on employee-owned phones, marking them with briefcase badges. This system allows companies to manage work-related applications without accessing personal information. It's distinct from simply signing into a second Gmail account.

Currently, Work Profiles have limitations with car integrations; for example, Microsoft Teams audio calls don't work if installed within a managed Work Profile. Google Meet also restricts upcoming meetings and call history from appearing on the dashboard from an active Work Profile. These restrictions can be inconvenient for professionals needing to join calls while driving.

The potential Work Mode switch on the dashboard could eventually allow users to silence work alerts during their commute home, leaving personal calls and navigation unaffected. This offers a convenient way to pause work apps and notifications without affecting personal use.

However, Google has not officially commented on whether Android Auto's experimental tile will offer these specific controls or when it might arrive. It hasn't been shown to pause notifications or launch work apps directly. Current Android Auto customization options do not bypass existing Work Profile restrictions.

Even if implemented, drivers might not get access to all company apps, as Android Auto restricts app capabilities while driving, and employers control app availability within Work Profiles. On company-owned devices, IT admins can also set limits on how long a Work Profile can remain paused, potentially affecting personal app access.

headline_marked: [[AI smart glasses can get prescription lenses]], but daily use faces major weight, battery, and privacy hurdles.
headline: AI smart glasses can get prescription lenses, but daily use faces major weight, battery, and privacy hurdles.
summary: While AI-powered smart glasses like Ray-Ban Meta can be fitted with prescription lenses, their suitability for daily use is hampered by increased weight, limited battery life, and significant privacy concerns leading to bans in various public and corporate set
details: AI-powered smart glasses, such as the Ray-Ban Meta, can be equipped with prescription lenses, allowing users to order them directly with their vision correction. This makes them technically capable of replacing traditional eyewear.
However, smart glasses are significantly heavier, weighing up to 80 grams compared to regular glasses' 20-30 grams. This added weight can become uncomfortable during all-day wear.

Battery life is another major limitation, with most AI glasses lasting only 3 to 5 hours on a single charge. Constant recharging would be necessary for full-day use, losing smart features when the battery dies.

Privacy is a critical concern, as many public and corporate environments have banned AI glasses due to their recording capabilities. Courts in England and Wales, New York, and numerous schools have implemented such prohibitions.

Even without active recording, features like real-time translation could upload confidential conversations to third-party servers. Meta has faced scrutiny over outsourced workers accessing intimate user content for product improvement.
The social aspect also plays a role, with users reporting fear of being labeled negatively due to the ongoing backlash against smart glasses. This has led some to stop wearing them in public.

Ultimately, despite the technical possibility of integrating prescription lenses, the combined issues of weight, battery life, privacy, and social perception position AI glasses as a secondary option rather than a practical replacement for everyday prescription eyewear.
